title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Rail
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: A CVSS 10 authentication bypass in Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center is under active exploitation — that box is the IT/OT boundary TSA asks you to prove
items.content_text: Cisco and CISA confirmed on 9 September that CVE-2026-20079 in Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center is under active exploitation. The flaw is a critical authentication bypass caused by an improper system process created at boot; a remote, unauthenticated attacker sends crafted HTTP requests and gains root on the appliance operating system. Cisco fixed it in early March and published indicators of compromise in late July, then disclosed on 9 September that it had observed exploitation from August. CISA added the CVE to KEV with a 12 September federal deadline, which has now passed. Cisco Talos tracks three clusters (its post was last revised on 21 September and still names the same three) of post-compromise activity across this flaw and the earlier CVE-2026-20316: UAT-12197, which used CVE-2026-20079 to plant a web shell and a JAR-based command executor and steal credentials; UAT-11823, an APT that used both flaws, whose tooling overlaps with Sandworm’s and which deployed a Cyclops Blink variant; and UAT-11988, which Talos assesses with high confidence to be a ransomware operator with TTPs consistent with Qilin affiliates; it got in only through the CVE-2026-20316 static credentials and deployed Qilin on selected endpoints. CVE-2026-20316 is not in the KEV catalogue. On 16 September Cisco shipped its September hardening release for ASA, FTD and FMC (CVE-2026-20329 to CVE-2026-20336, maximum CVSS 9.9), and revised the FMC advisory to replace the earlier hot fixes with those security-hardening builds (7.0.10, 7.2.12, 7.4.8, 7.6.6, 7.7.13, 10.0.2 and 10.1.0); there is no workaround. Nothing rail-specific has emerged since, and the item leads again only because no confirmed rail or transit incident displaced it. For railroads and transit agencies the consequence is specific. TSA security directives require a documented, tested separation between IT and critical cyber systems — dispatch, signalling support, traction-power SCADA, fare and station systems. FMC is where that separation is enforced, and root there lets an attacker edit it silently.

items.title: A suspected China-linked group stole SCADA and HMI source code from an automation vendor — the repositories were self-hosted, reachable and running an unpatched Gitea
items.content_text: Acronis threat intelligence published findings on 13 September on an actor it calls Red Heron, which has been exploiting CVE-2026-60004, a critical remote code execution flaw in self-hosted Gitea, since 29 July 2026. The group scanned 1,386 internet-facing Gitea instances across seven countries and confirmed compromises at 11 organisations in five countries, by Acronis’s count (some secondary reports give higher figures). Two victims matter here. A Taiwanese industrial-automation company lost repositories covering SCADA and HMI tooling, IoT platform integrations and network-sniffer products. A Canadian renewable-energy firm lost infrastructure maps, configuration secrets, SSH host keys and internal tokens. The toolset includes the JITTERLY Linux implant, a new self-restoring LD_PRELOAD rootkit Acronis calls SIXZUT, and the Adaptix C2 framework. Attribution to a Chinese-speaking group is moderate confidence, resting on language artefacts and tradecraft; the compromises themselves are confirmed. No rail organisation is among the named victims, but the exposure class is one transit owns outright: signalling, SCADA and passenger-information work is contracted out, and the contractor’s repository server holds the project files, controller logic and credentials for your estate.

items.title: Coordinated track sabotage stopped Dutch trains for a morning — physical, not cyber, and the fail-safe did exactly what it is designed to do
items.content_text: On the morning of Tuesday 15 September, the day of the Dutch state opening of parliament, ProRail found steel pipes up to two metres long fixed to the rails at somewhere between twenty and thirty locations, including the Amersfoort–Zwolle, Zwolle–Leeuwarden, Utrecht–Arnhem, Arnhem–Zutphen, Amersfoort–Deventer and Gouda–Oudewater lines. A pipe bridging the two rails shorts the track circuit, so the occupancy detection reports a train that is not there and the protecting signals hold at red. The first was found at about 05:30; one train struck a pipe near Steenwijk without injury; services north of Utrecht were worst affected, with knock-on disruption to German connections, and most of the network was restored by the afternoon. ProRail said the material had been placed intentionally; the AIVD intelligence service is working with police; no suspect has been named and a farmers’ protest group publicly denied involvement. This was physical sabotage with no reported cyber component, and it does not change the cyber threat level on this page. It is here because it is the only rail incident of the week and because the mechanism is instructive: an attacker who understood signalling chose to trigger the safety case rather than defeat it, and the result was delay rather than danger. That is the outcome a track circuit or axle counter is engineered to produce, and it is the same outcome a defender should expect from a well-designed vital system under most cyber conditions — a fail-safe stop, with the operational cost carried in disruption.

items.title: CISA publishes a cyber-decoys guide — detection you can add without touching a vital system
items.content_text: CISA released “Using Cyber Decoys to Strengthen Detection and Response” on 17 September. It defines decoys as assets that appear to be legitimate systems, accounts or data but exist to distract adversaries, reveal their presence and support threat-intelligence collection, and it sets out three phases — preparation, execution and analysis — positioning the technique alongside Zero Trust rather than as a replacement for it. The reason this matters more in rail than in most sectors is what it does not require. Decoys, honeytokens and tripwire accounts are additive: a credential that should never be used, a fake engineering share, a dummy historian tag, a service account that exists only to be alerted on. None of that changes a signalling, interlocking or traction-power system, which is normally the reason detection work stalls on a railway — the asset owner will not accept a change to a vital system for a monitoring benefit. This is guidance, not a threat item: no vulnerability, no incident and no product is involved.

items.title: August set a global ransomware record at 997 attacks, with utilities among the categories driving the rise
items.content_text: Comparitech data reported on 14 September recorded 997 ransomware attacks worldwide in August 2026 — an average of 32 a day, a 23 percent increase on July’s 809, and above the previous monthly record of 988. The reporting singles out utility, healthcare and business-services attacks as the categories behind the surge. Treat the absolute number with the usual caution — counts of this kind depend on leak-site claims and disclosure practice as much as on actual incident volume, and claimed victims are not confirmed victims. The direction of travel, however, is consistent with what operators are seeing. Transport and logistics organisations are part of the surge. For rail and transit the exposure is rarely the signalling system itself — it is dispatch support, crew management, maintenance planning, fare collection and passenger information, all of which can degrade service without any train control being touched.

items.title: Cyber-informed engineering argues the useful question is not how to keep attackers out, but which consequences you can design away
items.content_text: An analysis published 15 September sets out the case for cyber-informed engineering in critical infrastructure: that industrial systems operate under a constraint IT does not share, because a compromised network does not automatically have to become a catastrophic physical event. The argument is to move the security question upstream into design — identifying the physical consequences that actually matter, then engineering them out with controls that do not depend on the digital system remaining trustworthy. Rail has practised this for a century without calling it cybersecurity: interlocking, fail-safe signalling and vital logic exist precisely so that a failure upstream cannot produce an unsafe movement. The current argument is that those principles should be applied deliberately to digital systems rather than assumed to still hold. This is practitioner analysis rather than incident reporting; it names no victim and describes no attack, but it is the most useful lens available for operators whose detection budget will never match their consequence exposure.

items.title: An entire credential campaign, start to finish, in under six hours — Google documents autonomous agents doing the work
items.content_text: Google’s Threat Intelligence Group reported on 8 September that a financially motivated group completed a large-scale credential-harvesting campaign in less than six hours using an autonomous multi-agent framework, with the agents rather than human operators carrying it through. GTIG separately observed actors stealing AI API credentials and running unauthorised workloads inside victims’ own cloud tenants across healthcare, government and media. Its guidance is to assume every actor is now using AI to some degree. The rail consequence is arithmetic, not novelty. Credential phishing against dispatchers, crew callers, maintenance planners and contractor accounts is the standard opening move, and a campaign that completes inside six hours finishes well before a Monday-morning review — and comfortably inside the overnight window when the operations control centre is staffed but the security team is not.

items.title: Four more boundary products went into KEV on 22 September — Check Point VPN and management, Arista’s SD-WAN orchestrator and F5 APM, all due 25 September
items.content_text: CISA added four actively exploited flaws to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 22 September, each with a federal remediation deadline of 25 September. Two are Check Point’s, confirmed in Check Point’s own advisory the same day. CVE-2026-85102 (CVSS 9.8) is improper validation of certificate data during VPN negotiation on Security Gateways and Spark firewalls, giving unauthenticated remote code execution; the patch shipped on 9 September and Check Point says it observed a wave of exploitation attempts against Spark customers starting 12 September. CVE-2026-93616 (CVSS 9.8) is a separate, pre-authentication path traversal in the Security Management web service that allows script execution; Check Point describes a handful of pinpointed attacks on 23 July, so it was a zero-day for about two months, with the fix released on 22 September. The third is Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator, CVE-2026-93952 (CVSS 10.0), an input-validation flaw in on-premises orchestrators that Arista says is actively exploited; exposure requires certificate-based Edge-to-Orchestrator authentication, and hosted orchestrators are already patched. The fourth is F5 BIG-IP APM, CVE-2026-94127 (CVSS 9.8), an unauthenticated heap overflow reachable only where a virtual server combines an APM access policy with an OAuth profile, fixed by engineering hotfixes. No victim in any sector has been named and nothing ties these to rail. The rail fit is architectural: SD-WAN orchestrators push configuration to the edges in stations, depots and wayside communication huts; Check Point gateways often terminate supplier remote access; and the management server holds the policy that enforces the IT/OT separation TSA asks you to document.

items.title: A CVSS 9.8 flaw in the lwIP embedded network stack leads CISA’s 22 September batch — the question is which of your field devices ship its MQTT client
items.content_text: CISA published nine ICS advisories on 22 September: two for lwIP, the lightweight open-source TCP/IP stack built into a very wide range of embedded controllers, gateways, I/O modules and sensors; six for Siemens; and one for OpenPLC. The headline is ICSA-26-265-01, an out-of-bounds write in lwIP’s MQTT client application (CVE-2026-87121, CVSS 9.8 v3.1 and 9.3 v4.0, network-reachable with no authentication or user interaction) that may give an attacker full code execution on the device; it was reported by Shahriyar Jalayeri of ByteRay. ICSA-26-265-02 is a separate double free in lwIP, reported by Eric Evenchick of Tetrel Security; we could not verify its CVE or score, so none is quoted. Because lwIP is a library, the practical exposure depends on which device vendors compiled in the MQTT client, and no downstream vendor list had been published by 24 September. Two of the Siemens advisories touch station estates: an unrestricted file upload in Siveillance Control, Siemens’ physical-security management platform, and a code-injection flaw in the Desigo CC building-management family, reported by Michelin CERT. No exploitation is reported for any advisory in the batch. For rail, the plausible lwIP carriers are the telemetry gateways, condition-monitoring sensors and small controllers in traction-power, tunnel-ventilation and wayside cabinets, many of which publish over MQTT.

items.title: CISA adds a Zyxel GS1900 switch flaw to KEV after GreyNoise counts 996 compromised units — the kind of switch found in a station office, not a signal room
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-7273 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 21 September with a federal remediation deadline of 24 September. It is a stack-based buffer overflow in the CGI program of Zyxel GS1900-series managed switches (GS1900-8, 8HP, 10HP, 16, 24, 24E, 24EP, 24HPv2, 48 and 48HPv2) that lets an unauthenticated attacker with access to the management interface execute operating-system commands through a crafted HTTP request. Zyxel published the fix in June; its advisory gives no CVSS score and we do not supply one. The same day, GreyNoise published what it describes as the first documented in-the-wild exploitation: a single actor, active since May and assessed by GreyNoise as a Chinese speaker, exploited 996 GS1900 switches across 48 countries, including 129 in the United States and 66 in the Netherlands, using an obfuscated Python tool that pulled device configurations and root-level password hashes over TFTP; 564 of the victims were still on factory-default credentials. GreyNoise links the same actor to data theft from an unnamed western government organisation through two WordPress flaws, and infers an overlap with the Red Heron activity already on this page through shared infrastructure and malware — an inference, not an observation. No rail or transit victim is identified. Our assessment of the rail relevance: GS1900 is a small-office switch, and the place it turns up on a railway or transit property is the station back office, the yard office, the small agency’s headquarters LAN or a contractor’s site cabin, not the signalling or traction-power network. A compromised switch there yields a network foothold and every credential configured on it.

items.title: Three exploited Linux kernel flaws land in KEV with a three-day federal deadline — the question for rail is which appliances run Linux underneath
items.content_text: CISA added three Linux kernel vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 18 September, across two alerts, with a federal remediation deadline of 21 September, which has now passed; no further exploitation detail has been published since the listing. CVE-2025-39682 is in the kernel TLS receive path, where a zero-length record can bypass record-type handling. CVE-2026-53266 is an out-of-bounds write in the netfilter bridge ebtables SNAT target, which can lead to memory corruption, denial of service or local privilege escalation on hosts with bridge netfilter rules configured. CVE-2025-39964 is a race condition in the AF_ALG crypto socket interface, exploitable by a local, low-privileged user. Published severity scores for the three differ widely between sources, so none is quoted here. CISA lists them as exploited in the wild, but no public detail says who is exploiting them or against what, and none is tied to a rail or OT target. None is a rail product. As with the Linux kernel addition of 27 August, the relevance is that traffic-management servers, passenger information systems, CCTV recorders and many wayside and on-board gateways run Linux underneath, often as vendor appliances patched on the supplier’s schedule. These are local, post-access bugs that let an attacker who already has a foothold go further, not ways in from the internet.

items.title: A CVSS 10.0 authentication bypass in Cisco Identity Services Engine is being exploited — that is the box deciding who gets onto which network
items.content_text: Cisco published advisory cisco-sa-ISE-ABP-VNSW7Tn5 on 16 September for CVE-2026-76460, a CVSS 10.0 flaw in Identity Services Engine and ISE-PIC. An API endpoint with insufficient authentication lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker bypass the web-based management interface, and Cisco states that its PSIRT is aware of active exploitation. All versions are affected; fixes are 3.1 Patch 12, 3.2 Patch 11, 3.3 Patch 12, 3.4 Patch 7 and 3.5 Patch 4. There are no workarounds — restricting management traffic with infrastructure access control lists is the only mitigation Cisco offers. CISA added the CVE to the KEV catalogue on 16 September with a three-day federal deadline of 19 September, which has now passed. No actor attribution has been published, and no critical-infrastructure or OT targeting has been claimed; Singapore’s Cyber Security Agency reinforced the advisory with its own alert on 21 September. ISE 3.0 is end-of-life and gets no fix, so those deployments must migrate. The rail relevance is structural rather than reported: ISE is the network access control and policy engine many railroads and transit authorities use to decide which port, VLAN and remote session a device or contractor is allowed, including the segmentation between corporate systems and dispatch, signalling support, traction-power SCADA and station estates. Root over the policy engine is root over the boundary. Separately, CISA added Cisco Secure Email Gateway CVE-2026-76461 to KEV on 14 September, due 17 September — a second exploited Cisco entry point in the same week.

items.title: Moxa fixes an unauthenticated crash in the web login of its TN-4500B switches — a line it markets for rolling-stock networks
items.content_text: Moxa published security advisory MPSA-252620 on 18 September for CVE-2026-15579 in its TN-4500B Ethernet switch series, a line Moxa markets for rolling-stock networks: its product page describes the ToughNet TN-4500B switches as designed for railway applications including rolling stock, and as meeting the EN 50155 test requirements. The flaw is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) in the web login: the username field is not length-checked, so a remote, unauthenticated attacker who can reach the web interface can send an overlong value and crash the authentication process. The impact Moxa describes is denial of service, with no confidentiality loss; it scores the flaw CVSS v4 8.8 (vector AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:L/VA:H) and rates it High. Firmware v2.0 and earlier is affected and v2.1 or later fixes it. The advisory makes no statement about exploitation, and we found no report of attacks. Our assessment of the rail relevance: switches of this class usually sit inside the train, carrying the on-board network, so the reachable question is which vehicle networks and train-to-ground links expose the switch’s web management at all.

items.title: Twenty-two flaws in Pepperl+Fuchs IO-Link masters, two of them CVSS 9.8 and unauthenticated — the same firmware ships under Phoenix Contact and Carlo Gavazzi badges
items.content_text: CERT@VDE published VDE-2026-014 on 16 September for 22 vulnerabilities in the firmware of Pepperl+Fuchs ICE2-8IOL and ICE3-8IOL IO-Link master modules, found by Nozomi Networks researchers. Firmware below 1.7.4 is affected and 1.7.8 fixes them. The two worst are CVE-2026-27546, an authentication bypass, and CVE-2026-27565, an unauthenticated upload of a malicious IODD device-description file that executes shell scripts, both CVSS v3.1 9.8. The remainder (CVE-2026-27547 to -27564) are command-injection, file-inclusion and authorisation flaws between 7.2 and 8.8 that lead to root-level code execution; CVE-2026-27557 (7.5) is an unauthenticated path traversal that reads the SSH server’s private keys, and CVE-2026-27553 (6.5) discloses password hashes. Because the firmware is shared, Phoenix Contact IOL MA8 PN DI8 and IOL MA8 EIP DI8 modules (VDE-2026-027, 20 CVEs) and Carlo Gavazzi YL212 and YN115 masters (VDE-2026-028) carry the same fixes on the same date. No exploitation is reported and no CISA advisory had appeared by 22 September. The rail relevance is our assessment rather than anything in the advisory: IO-Link masters sit at the sensor and actuator layer of discrete automation, which on a railway means depot and workshop equipment, wheel lathes, wash plants, material-handling and platform plant supplied by integrators, usually on PROFINET or EtherNet/IP segments the operator’s IT team has never inventoried. Nothing here touches signalling or train control.

items.title: Seven new ICS advisories and one update on 17 September — one of them a transport device, none of them exploited
items.content_text: CISA published seven new advisories, ICSA-26-260-01 through -07, plus one update, on Thursday 17 September; the next batch followed on 22 September and is carried as a separate card. The advisory carrying CISA’s Transportation Systems label is ICSA-26-260-01, covering Bransys ELD for Android below 11.00.00 and for iOS below 1.1.54: hard-coded MQTT credentials (CVE-2026-86520, CVSS 7.5), cleartext transmission of sensitive information (CVE-2026-86689, 5.9) and hard-coded FTP credentials (CVE-2026-77960, 5.3), all fixed in the versions named. These are electronic logging devices for commercial road vehicles, so for a railroad or transit authority the exposure sits with fleet, maintenance-of-way and non-revenue vehicle telematics rather than anywhere near train control — it should not be read as a rail advisory. The most significant score in the batch is ICSA-26-260-02, a Mitsubishi Electric authentication-algorithm flaw in GX Works3 and Motion Control Settings affecting all versions (CVE-2026-15688, CVSS 8.8 v3.1 and 8.7 v4.0), which allows a local authentication bypass and tampering with control programs — relevant to workshop, depot and maintenance-facility automation. The remaining five cover Hitachi Energy FACTS Control Platform (-03, whose score we could not verify, so none is quoted), Schneider Electric Modicon M340 and X80 Ethernet communication modules (-04, CVE-2025-6625, a denial of service through a crafted FTP command, CVSS 7.5 v3.1 and 8.7 v4, fixed in M340 firmware SV3.70; a republication of Schneider’s 2025 advisory), Schneider Electric NetBotz 5 750 and 755 (-05, CVE-2026-13336 command injection at 6.4 v3.1 and 7.3 v4, plus CVE-2026-13337, fixed in 5.6.0), ABB Ability Edgenius (-06, the “Copy Fail” Linux kernel flaw CVE-2026-31431 at 7.8, fixed in 3.2.4.1) and Schneider Electric PowerChute Serial Shutdown (-07, CVE-2026-13348, excessive authentication attempts, 5.3 v3.1 and 6.9 v4; see the vendor advisory for the fixed version). CISA also updated ICSA-26-211-07 (Mitsubishi CC-Link IE TSN) on 17 September to add eight affected products. No exploitation is reported for anything in the batch.

items.title: Rockwell extends its lockout-recovery guidance to Micro820 and Micro850 — the small PLCs attackers were found setting passwords on
items.content_text: Rockwell Automation published revision 5.0 of security notice SD1790 on 18 September, its fifth revision since the notice first appeared on 30 July. The notice exists because of an FBI public service announcement of 30 July describing attackers who remotely altered the configuration of internet-exposed programmable logic controllers, changed IP addresses and set passwords where none had existed, locking the operators out. The original guidance covered MicroLogix 1100 and 1400; revision 5.0 extends the hardening and password-recovery instructions to the Micro820 and Micro850 controllers as well. There is no CVE: the notice is about exposure and configuration, not a software flaw. The controls Rockwell lists are the familiar ones — remove the controller from any internet-reachable path, put access behind a VPN and firewall, set strong passwords, keep offline backups of the project so a locked controller can be restored, disable the built-in HTTP server and keep firmware current. The revision adds no new incident data. Our assessment of the rail relevance: MicroLogix and Micro800-class controllers are the low-cost PLCs that end up in small, distributed installations built by contractors — pump and drainage stations, tunnel and station plant, yard equipment, small traction-power auxiliaries — often with a cellular modem for remote support and no entry in the operator’s OT asset register. The FBI describes a class of attack that needs no exploit at all, just reachability.

items.title: ConnectWise ScreenConnect joins KEV with attackers already pushing scripts to endpoints as they connect — the second remote-support console in five days
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-84869 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 11 September. It is a missing-authorisation flaw in ConnectWise ScreenConnect, scored CVSS 9.9, that permits unauthorised file transfer and code execution, and three separate incidents are documented in which threat actors abused it to push malicious scripts to endpoints at the moment those endpoints connected. A patch is available and the federal remediation deadline was 14 September. Arriving five days after N-able N-central landed in the same catalogue at CVSS 10.0, this is the same failure twice inside a week, in the two consoles third parties most often use to reach industrial estates. ScreenConnect in particular travels in the field-service bag: signalling contractors, fare-collection vendors, SCADA integrators and building-systems suppliers install it to support what they commissioned, frequently without a change record, and frequently on machines that also talk to the operational network.

items.title: GitLab CVSS 10 path traversal is being exploited, and rail and transit teams host more of it than they think
items.content_text: GitLab patched CVE-2026-85706 on 10 September, a path-traversal flaw in the repository commits API that it rated CVSS 10.0 and that allows an unauthenticated attacker to read arbitrary files from a GitLab server. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Friday 11 September with a remediation deadline for federal agencies of Monday 14 September. watchTowr reported it was already seeing in-the-wild probes for vulnerable servers, and Hong Kong’s CERT issued its own advisory on 14 September stating the flaw is being exploited in the wild. A second flaw fixed in the same release, CVE-2026-87719, can expose sensitive information from Enterprise Edition servers. Passenger and freight operators keep dispatch, CAD/AVL, passenger-information, fare-collection and back-office signalling support code in self-hosted GitLab instances that often sit on the corporate side with routed paths into the operational network. Unauthenticated file reads expose the credentials and integration detail that bridge those two worlds.

items.title: CISA flags a CVSS 9.8 missing-authorisation flaw in mySCADA myPRO Manager — and lists Transportation among the sectors running it
items.content_text: CISA published ICSA-26-258-03 on 15 September covering mySCADA myPRO Manager version 2.1 and earlier. It carries two flaws: CVE-2026-73807, a missing-authorisation vulnerability scored CVSS v3 9.8, and CVE-2026-82567, missing authentication for a critical function, scored 6.3. Together they could let an attacker reach privileged management functions or send arbitrary SMS messages through a GSM modem connected to the system. mySCADA has fixed both in version 2.2. CISA lists the deployed sectors as Critical Manufacturing, Energy, Food and Agriculture, Transportation and Water, and states that no known public exploitation targeting these flaws has been reported to it. No rail or transit deployment is named in the advisory. The relevance here is inventory: small SCADA and HMI packages turn up in station plant, pumping, tunnel ventilation and depot systems commissioned by integrators, and an SMS-capable modem on such a system is often the alarm path to on-call staff.

items.title: Nozomi’s SCALANCE LPE9403 research now runs to twelve flaws, several chainable to root on an OT edge device — vendor-patched and unexploited
items.content_text: Nozomi Networks Labs published the second part of its Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403 research on 18 September, taking the disclosed set to twelve vulnerabilities: nine in the device firmware, scored CVSS 5.3 to 8.5, and three in the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client, scored 6.7 to 8.5. The first part, published 10 September, covered four memory-corruption flaws in the PROFINET Discovery and basic Configuration Protocol implementation — CVE-2025-40575 through CVE-2025-40578, each CVSS 5.3 — where a daemon running as root, unauthenticated and bound to every device interface can be crashed with crafted Ethernet frames from the same Layer 2 segment. The material addition in part two is that Nozomi demonstrates several of the flaws chaining to root-level control of the device, which would allow telemetry to be manipulated, alarms suppressed, operational data read, OT services disrupted and lateral movement attempted from the edge node. This is disclosed research on vendor-patched issues rather than a new critical exposure: the CVEs carry 2025 identifiers, Siemens has published fixes, the affected versions are LPE9403 firmware below V4.0 HF0 and SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client through V2.1, and CISA’s update of the existing advisory ICSA-25-135-18 to version 4 on 15 September added the Edge Client and the vendor fixes. There is no evidence of exploitation in the wild. Rail and transit estates running the LPE9403 as an edge processing node in depots, traction power rooms or station plant rooms should treat this as a firmware-currency question: the realistic worst case is not a crash but an edge device that keeps reporting normally while under someone else’s control.

items.title: N-able N-central lands in KEV at CVSS 10 — the console many transit and short-line IT providers run
items.content_text: CISA added four actively exploited vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 8 September. The lead item is CVE-2026-86218 in N-able N-central, a static code injection flaw scored CVSS 10.0 that yields pre-authentication remote code execution. N-able confirmed exploitation in the wild, Huntress observed attacks against N-central’s API and appliance logs from 4 September, and N-able shipped 2026.3 Hotfix 4 on 5 September — its fourth hotfix in five weeks. The federal remediation deadline was 11 September and has now passed. N-central is a remote monitoring and management platform: an agent with system-level rights on every managed endpoint, operated by a third party. Short lines, commuter authorities and municipal transit agencies commonly outsource back-office IT to providers running exactly this console. Also added were two Windows zero-days granting SYSTEM and an Adobe Commerce injection flaw.

items.title: NetScaler and FortiOS are confirmed exploited and in KEV — the two boxes most often standing between a supplier and a rail OT network
items.content_text: CISA added two more edge products to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 9 September. The first is an authentication bypass in Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway, CVE-2026-19490 at CVSS 9.3, affecting AAA virtual server and Gateway configurations; honeypot telemetry recorded 56 exploitation attempts from 3 September, 36 of them on 8 September alone. The second is a heap buffer overflow in Fortinet FortiOS, FortiSwitchManager and FortiSASE, CVE-2025-25249 at CVSS 7.3, exploited since July 2026 in a campaign distributing the PivotC2 remote access trojan that has reached more than 3,000 addresses, with an estimated 178 FortiGate devices found infected and the concentration in the United States. Both carried a federal remediation deadline of 12 September, now passed. This supersedes the August NetScaler item previously carried here. Neither of these is an IT asset in any useful sense for a railroad: the NetScaler gateway is how the signalling supplier gets in, and the FortiGate is often the only device between the corporate network and a dispatch or SCADA segment.

items.title: CERT Polska confirms the MikroTik “MikroTrick” chain is now being exploited — the router class that quietly backhauls remote rail sites
items.content_text: CERT Polska issued an alert on 9 September confirming that the MikroTik RouterOS vulnerability chain known as “MikroTrick”, previously disclosed but not confirmed exploited, is now being used in real-world attacks observed since at least 2 September. The chain pairs an SSH authentication-bypass flaw, CVE-2026-67276 at CVSS 9.2, with an SSH privilege-escalation flaw, CVE-2026-86060 also at CVSS 9.2, to take full unauthenticated administrative control of an internet-exposed RouterOS device. A third bug, CVE-2026-67277, allows memory disclosure or denial of service through the bandwidth-test service. CERT Polska named no victims and no sectors, describing only the exposure category: MikroTik devices are widely deployed by internet service providers, data centres, enterprises and critical-infrastructure networks. Nothing in the alert ties the activity to rail or transit. The relevance for this audience is inventory rather than attribution — low-cost RouterOS hardware is a common choice for backhaul at remote, unstaffed sites such as crossings, wayside cabinets, yard offices and small stations, and a router compromised at that layer sits upstream of whatever segmentation you rely on.

items.title: September’s ICS patch round lands on Modicon controllers, RTUs and the protection relays behind traction power
items.content_text: Schneider Electric published four advisories on 8 September, the most severe a critical authentication vulnerability in the Modicon M580 and Modicon M580 Safety controllers, CVE-2026-3869 at CVSS 9.2. Also fixed: high-severity flaws in the PowerLogic T300 RTU — formerly the Easergy T300, a distribution-automation RTU that turns up in traction-power and substation retrofits — and in EcoStruxure IT Data Center Expert, plus a medium-severity SCADAPack x70 defect. Siemens issued nine advisories, seven on 8 September, headlined by ProductCERT SSA-142885: fourteen CVEs in Reyrolle 7SR5 protection and control relays for all versions before V2.70, led by CVE-2026-62645 (CVSS v3.1 9.8), where the web interface leaks enough data to calculate current and past session identifiers and bypass authentication. Siemens also patched Industrial Edge Management and Open Interface Services, and Aveva fixed four flaws in the PIMBoards component of Pipeline Integrity Monitor, which CISA published on 10 September as ICSA-26-253-01: a hardcoded cryptographic key (CVE-2026-81821) and a weak password-hashing algorithm (CVE-2026-81822), both CVSS v3 8.4, plus a missing-authorisation flaw (CVE-2026-81823, 5.3) and a cross-site scripting flaw (CVE-2026-81824, 4.7), all fixed in 2025 SP1 P2. That product is an oil-and-gas pipeline leak-detection tool rather than a rail one, and is listed here for completeness of the September round. CISA republished the Reyrolle 7SR5 advisory as ICSA-26-258-05 and the SCADAPack x70 advisory as ICSA-26-258-04 on 15 September. No exploitation is reported for any of it.

items.title: CISA’s Cyber Storm X put a nation-state attack on rail and ports at the centre of the national exercise — the after-action report is the part worth waiting for
items.content_text: CISA announced on 22 September that it had run Cyber Storm X, the tenth in its national cyber exercise series: four days, about 2,000 participants from more than 200 federal, state, local and private-sector organisations, built around a nation-state adversary targeting the transportation systems sector, with rail and ports named, and the water and wastewater sector. The stated objectives were to test response plans, practise coordination and information sharing, and examine roles and responsibilities under national-level cyber plans. Acting CISA Director Nick Andersen said exercises make sure “our plans, policies, and partnerships are ready when we need them.” CISA says it will publish a public after-action report with observations, analyses and recommendations. The exercise dates were not given in the coverage we could read. This is preparedness, not an incident, and it does not move the threat level on this page; it is here because a scenario that places rail inside a national nation-state playbook is the closest thing to sector-specific federal attention this week.

items.title: CISA retires its weekly vulnerability bulletin on 28 September — check whether it is anyone’s only feed
items.content_text: CISA is discontinuing its weekly Vulnerability Summary bulletin with effect from 28 September, reported on 17 September, and is pointing readers to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue and to its alerts and advisories instead. The change is framed as consistent with the risk-based prioritisation set out in binding operational directive BOD 26-04 of June 2026: a weekly list of everything published is a poor substitute for a shorter list of what is actually being exploited. Nothing in the reporting indicates that ICS advisories are affected. For rail the practical question is narrow and worth asking this week. Larger railroads run vulnerability management from vendor feeds and commercial intelligence and will not notice. Short lines, terminal railroads and smaller transit authorities sometimes have exactly one person who reads exactly one weekly email, and if that email is this one, the replacement needs to be arranged before the end of the month rather than discovered in October.

items.title: ENISA switches on the Single Reporting Platform as the Cyber Resilience Act’s vulnerability reporting duties take effect
items.content_text: The EU Agency for Cybersecurity deployed the initial operating capability of its Single Reporting Platform, announced 14 September, giving manufacturers and open-source software stewards the channel they need to meet Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligations that took effect this month. Under the CRA, makers of products with digital elements must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents on a defined clock, with an early warning followed by a fuller notification. Rail operators are largely beneficiaries rather than regulated parties, but rolling-stock, signalling and passenger-system suppliers selling into the EU now carry the reporting duty, and their disclosure timelines should tighten accordingly. Reported here factually as a regulatory milestone, without comment on the underlying policy debate.

items.title: TSA reopens its surface-transportation cyber information collection — and the vetting rule for coordinators has changed
items.content_text: TSA published a Federal Register notice on 1 September covering the revised information collection for higher-risk freight rail, mass transit and passenger rail, and over-the-road bus owners and operators, with comments due 1 October 2026. The collection carries forward the substance of the security directives rather than replacing it: designated primary and alternate cybersecurity coordinators, 72-hour incident reporting to CISA, a Cybersecurity Incident Response Plan, and Cybersecurity Implementation and Assessment Plans with annual assessment reports. One change is worth flagging to HR and legal now — introduced in the 15 January 2026 revision of SD 1580-21-01 and SD 1582-21-01, a cybersecurity coordinator who is not a US citizen must hold NEXUS, Global Entry or equivalent TSA-approved vetting. TSA also re-estimated the burden at 67 respondents and 22,167 hours, down from 846 and 210,684.

items.title: 117 federal incident-reporting rules across 27 agencies — and a transit agency can sit inside several clocks at once
items.content_text: The McCrary Institute and the US Chamber of Commerce published analysis on 8 September, citing GAO work, counting 117 federal cyber incident reporting regulations across 27 agencies, 48 of which reach private industry. The argument is operational rather than political: filings with different thresholds, formats and deadlines pull the same small group of people away from containment during the hours that matter most. Rail sits in an unusually crowded corner of that map. A single event at a transit authority can trigger the 72-hour report to CISA required under the TSA security directives, an FTA or state safety oversight notification, a local emergency-management report, a breach notification if rider or payment data is involved, and — once CIRCIA rules are finalised, expected this autumn — a further CISA filing on its own clock.
